title: A case against the “Education Revolution”
author: Paul Matthews
summary: Paul Matthews argues that calls to revolutionise education because of AI are like burning down your house because you need new carpet. He grants that a great deal has changed, citing Neil Postman's point that technological change is ecological, so schools are now different rather than old schools plus ChatGPT, and he lists changes in tools, jobs, outsourcing, sources of information and speed of change. His thesis is that the most important things in education have not changed: the purpose of schooling as forming people rather than producing work, who a learner is, how people learn through effort and prior knowledge, how the brain works, and what good teaching looks like. He supports the case for naming constants with a 2019 Academy of Management Journal study finding people more willing to back change when leaders also say what will stay the same, especially under high uncertainty. His practical message to school leaders, teachers and students is to bring the unchanging truths front and centre and pursue renovation, not revolution.
points: The carpet metaphor frames the right response to AI as repairing the part that is worn out rather than demolishing the whole system.
Matthews concedes real change in tools, graduate jobs, outsourcing, information sources and pace, using Postman to argue schools are now different rather than merely augmented.
His list of constants (purpose, the learner as a whole person, effortful learning, how the brain works, and good teaching) gives leaders a concrete inventory to defend and communicate.

Research from the Academy of Management Journal suggests staff support change more readily when leaders articulate what will stay the same, making this a change-management tactic and not a soft option.
quotes: Revolutionising” education because of AI is like burning down your house because you need new carpet.
Much of what matters most in education hasn’t changed at all.

Technological change is not additive; it is ecological... A new medium does not add something; it changes everything. In the year 1500, after the printing press was invented, you did not have old Europe plus the printing press. You had a different Europe.
The purpose of education. Schools are still producing people, not producing work. The aim of a school was never the essay; it was the formation of the student writing it.
Attention is finite, memory is the residue of thought, and the brain still takes the easy path whenever it’s offered. AI didn’t create that tendency. It just made the easy path shorter.
People were more willing to support change when leaders also articulated what would stay the same. And the effect was strongest when uncertainty was highest.
When all we talk about is revolution, our staff hear that everything they value is up for grabs, and they can often dig in and resist change.
Being clear about what isn’t changing is less about avoiding change and more about managing change wisely.
